description: Yttrium is a silvery-metallic transition metal with symbol Y and atomic number 39 that is chemically similar to the lanthanides and is often classified as a rare-earth element. It is a soft, lustrous and highly crystalline metal that is almost always found in combination with lanthanide elements in rare-earth minerals and is never found in nature as a free element. The pure element is relatively stable in air in bulk form due to a protective oxide film, but when finely divided, it is very unstable and can ignite at temperatures exceeding 400 °C.
uses: The most important present-day use of yttrium is as a component of phosphors, especially those used in LEDs, and historically it was widely used in red phosphors in television cathode ray tube displays. Yttrium is also used in the production of electrodes, electrolytes, electronic filters, lasers, superconductors, various medical applications, and for tracing materials to enhance their properties.
characteristics: Yttrium is a soft, silvery-metallic, lustrous and highly crystalline metal in group 3 that is less electronegative than scandium but has significantly stronger similarities to the lanthanides than to its periodic table neighbors. The pure element forms a protective Y2O3 oxide film on its surface that can reach 10 μm thickness when heated to 750 °C in water vapor, and it exists almost exclusively in the +3 oxidation state forming various inorganic compounds. Yttrium's Y3+ ion is colorless in solution due to the absence of electrons in the d and f electron shells.
